gradeResolution.basis: Explicit NONBLIND source/anchor adjudication after saving toub-third-34.json; this is not a fourth independent vote. Preserve originals32-verify level4/violin3/medium, originals32-blind level2/violin1/medium, and toub-third-34 level3/violin3/medium. The supported band is 2–4. Choose 3 from technical evidence, not averaging: the full score shows violin3 changing at V (m249, p16) to a repeated low E4-to-A5 leap followed by G5-F5-E5-D5-C5, with comparable register changes later exchanged among inner/lower parts. These repeated shifts/string transfers at sixteenth=384/min and the sustained nine-minute texture warrant upper-intermediate control beyond grading only the low first-violin scale. The level2 review correctly identifies moderate tempo, simple rhythm and lack of double stops/specialist bowing but overweights violin1 duration when naming the hardest part; sampled compact register does not dispose of the recurring A5 leap. The level4 review correctly selects violin3 and recognizes stamina/register changes, but its broad upper-register/endurance account does not identify the extra advanced technical vocabulary normally needed to distinguish early advanced from upper intermediate. A5 is manageable with ordinary intermediate position work; patterns are strongly repetitive, mostly scalar, in unchanged 2/4 and treble clef, with no rapid mixed rhythms, chords, double stops or prescribed virtuoso bow strokes. Late accidental changes increase finger-pattern vigilance but do not create a new higher register or speed tier. Thus 3 is a supported central technical placement with adjacent-level uncertainty; retain medium advisory confidence without upgrade. No ensemble-count uplift, no professional-performer grade inference. Source/date facts already verified remain preserved: do not resolve 2017 score/title versus 2012 album metadata or infer a live quartet from the stated human multitrack.

gradeResolution.basis: Explicit NONBLIND source adjudication of the three preserved opinions, not a fourth vote or median. The level-3 verify opinion correctly identifies compound-meter articulation demands but names the higher melodic line without isolating the true peak. My saved blind level-3 opinion correctly identifies Viola 4 as hardest but underreads its register: its claim that Viola 4 stays approximately C4-Eb5 is contradicted by Loekie Blues printed p.6 bars 79-80. Reinspection at larger scale confirms the accented ascending chromatic figure extends well above the treble staff, approximately D6 at its peak, in separate eighth-note attacks at dotted-quarter 116 (about 348 eighths/minute); Viola 5 doubles the gesture lower. This is upper-position viola writing, not alto-clef middle-register notation. Viola 4 also has the sustained chromatic semiquaver counterlines and alternating slurred/detached articulation of Slow Blues Song printed pp.12-14 bars 29-46, and the short four-note tuplets and chromatic offbeats in De Stille at dotted-quarter 124. The grades opinion therefore supplies the stronger hardest-part/register evidence and level 5 is retained within the actual 3-5 band. Relative anchor: level 3 ABRSM6/RCM7 understates secure upper-position rapid chromatic intonation plus rhythmic independence; level 5 ABRSM8/RCM9 better describes preparing that hardest part across the complete ten-minute set. This is a medium-confidence advisory teaching comparison, not official exam placement, with roughly one-level uncertainty. The brief high passages and abundant simpler writing prevent a further diploma-level claim; no uplift comes merely from eight players.

consideredOpinionDetails.basis: All 28 PDF pages inspected, including all 25 notation pages and three complete movements. Score is unusually written in treble clef for all eight viola staves (individual eighth part also supplied in alto/bass layouts). Mostly single-line writing in ordinary low/middle register; dotted compound-meter patterns at dotted-quarter 116, accents/offbeats, chromatic blues notes and quick arco/pizzicato changes determine the challenge. Slow Blues Song needs sustained bow control; De Stille at quarter124 uses repeated rhythmic figures. Viola1/5 upper melodic line slightly leads difficulty; no extreme register, extended techniques or elaborate double stopping. Upper intermediate 3, adjacent2–4 plausible. Advisory teaching estimate against data/source/levels.json, approximately one level either side; no automatic uplift for ensemble size.

Independent visual review of the complete Version A score, all three blues movements (PDF pp.4–28, printed pp.1–25). The hardest combined demands fall in viola 4: Loekie Blues includes exposed chromatic rising figures and a brief excursion above the treble staff around bars 79–83; Slow Blues Song adds active chromatic semiquaver figures with mixed slurred and detached articulation; De Stille requires crisp offbeat attacks, chromatic runs and occasional four-note tuplets at dotted-quarter=124. Much of the set is simpler, but the peak register and clean rapid articulation support advanced rather than an average of all eight parts. Repetition requires sustained rhythmic discipline, while rests reduce endurance pressure. No automatic eight-player uplift. Medium advisory estimate within one level; not exhaustive note certification.

Blind assessment before opening either existing review. Inspected all 28 PDF pages (three introductory pages and all 25 score pages), treating all three movements as one approximately ten-minute work. Viola 4 is the principal technical bottleneck rather than the highest line: Loekie Blues printed pp.5-6, bars 61-89 has the mobile chromatic counterline and accented rising figures; Slow blues song pp.12-14, bars 29-46 has sustained chromatic sixteenth-note runs, mixed slur/staccato, leaps, and displaced accents, shared closely with Viola 3; De Stille pp.18 and 24 adds chromatic four-note tuplets against compound pulse. All eight staves are printed in treble clef, including low ledger-line C-string material; this is a reading burden, not evidence of high-position playing. Overall register runs approximately C3 to F5; Viola 4 stays roughly C4-Eb5. The upper lines and Viola 5 reach higher but chiefly use simpler melody. Compound 6/8, offbeat entries, ties over beats, alternating pizzicato/arco, mute changes, chromatic blues intonation and precise dynamic/articulation coordination support upper-intermediate level 3. Dotted-quarter 116/66/124 gives brisk outer-movement eighth notes but the densest sustained sixteenths occur in the slow movement. No pervasive double stops, harmonics, advanced bowing or extreme register; eight players alone does not lift the grade. Teaching estimate anchored to supplied level 3 ABRSM6/RCM7 band, not an official syllabus placement.

gradeResolution.scope: musical-only nonblind adjudication; not an independent fourth vote
gradeResolution.basis: Level 4 is supported by the actual score, rather than selected simply because it lies between the three opinions. All three reviewers identify essentially the same notation; the disagreement concerns the weight placed on the first violin’s register, tempo and cumulative demands. Reinspection of the complete imposed score and enlarged printed p14 (Finale, especially mm184–235) shows recurring high-register attacks and slurred/detached quaver patterns, including the high E-register climax around m220, but these are short, largely sequential gestures with rests and returns to a settled position, rather than sustained rapid high-position passagework. Printed p10, Larghetto mm25–40, confirms chromatic semiquaver/demisemiquaver decoration within the slow 6/8 movement: fine print and many accidentals here do not imply a fast technical etude. I (pp3–7) is predominantly cantabile crotchet/minim writing; II (pp8–9) adds fast detached crotchets, leaps, coordinated rests and contrasting Trio phrasing. First violin remains the hardest part. The upper ledger-line register and repeated clean attacks/shifts across Scherzo and Finale warrant more than the level-3 Telemann sans-basse/Corelli Op5 No8 band; treating the largely regular rhythms and simpler accompaniments as decisive, as the level-3 reading does, underweights that recurring first-violin requirement. My original level-5 opinion placed too much weight on four-movement accumulation, chromaticism and the visual frequency of high notes. Those facts require secure early-advanced control but do not, at the written tempo contexts and pattern lengths, establish a consistent step beyond the local level-4 Bach Double/Haydn Op33 No2 anchors toward the level-5 La Folia/Haydn Rider band. The level-4 opinion makes the best-supported distinction between accessible note patterns and exposed execution. Ensemble balance, chromatic intonation and staggered entries are meaningful but regular enough to receive no additional uplift. Medium confidence retains about one level of uncertainty for chosen Vivace/Allegro assai tempo and required polish; no factual discrepancy or unresolved score identity prevents this musical judgment.
